claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by the formation and stability of a protective surface oxide scale.
An oxidizing atmosphere produces a continuous and adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3-rich surface layer.
The Al2O3/Cr2O3-rich layer limits oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Limiting oxygen ingress preserves the fcc matrix and mechanical integrity during oxidizing exposure.
Under hydrogen-dominated reducing conditions, the protective oxide scale forms incompletely or becomes destabilized.
Incomplete or destabilized oxide scales permit oxygen penetration through defects or along grain boundaries.
Oxygen penetration under reducing exposure causes internal oxidation along microstructural features such as grain boundaries.
Internal oxidation causes degradation of mechanical properties.
The as-fabricated additively manufactured alloy has a homogeneous fcc matrix.
The as-fabricated alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The as-fabricated alloy has minimal pre-existing surface oxidation.
Synergistic effects between Al and Cr promote rapid formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent protective oxide layer.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a uniform protective scale and limited internal oxidation.
Oxidizing exposure will cause only a minor change in mechanical performance relative to the as-fabricated state.
Reducing exposure will produce discontinuous or thicker and less-protective oxide features.
Reducing exposure will cause more internal oxidation and measurable fatigue-strength or hardness degradation than oxidizing exposure.
The proposed oxide-controlled degradation regime applies around 900 degrees Celsius in oxygen-rich or hydrogen-rich atmospheres.
